{{Short description|Formulation of classical mechanics}}
{{classical mechanics|Formulations}}

In [[classical mechanics]], '''Appell's equation of motion''' (a.k.a. the '''Gibbs–Appell equation of motion''') is an alternative general formulation of [[classical mechanics]] described by  [[Josiah Willard Gibbs]] in 1879<ref name="gibbs1879">{{cite journal|last=Gibbs|first=JW|year=1879|title=On the Fundamental Formulae of Dynamics.|journal=American Journal of Mathematics|volume=2|issue=1|pages=49&ndash;64|doi=10.2307/2369196|jstor=2369196}}</ref> and [[Paul Émile Appell]] in 1900.<ref name="appell_1900a">{{cite journal | last = Appell | first = P | year = 1900 | title = Sur une forme générale des équations de la dynamique.  | journal = Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik | volume = 121 | pages = 310&ndash;? }}</ref>

== Statement ==
The Gibbs-Appell equation reads

:<math>Q_{r} = \frac{\partial S}{\partial \alpha_{r}}, </math>

where <math>\alpha_r = \ddot{q}_r</math> is an arbitrary generalized acceleration, or the second time derivative of the [[generalized coordinate]]s <math>q_r </math>, and <math>Q_r </math> is its corresponding [[generalized force]]. The generalized force gives the work done

:<math>dW = \sum_{r=1}^{D} Q_{r} dq_{r}, </math>

where the index <math>r </math> runs over the <math>D </math> generalized coordinates <math>q_r </math>, which usually correspond to the [[degrees of freedom (physics and chemistry)|degrees of freedom]] of the system.  The function <math>S </math> is defined as the mass-weighted sum of the particle [[acceleration]]s squared,

:<math>S = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{N} m_{k} \mathbf{a}_{k}^{2}\,,</math>

where the index <math>k </math> runs over the <math>K </math> particles, and

:<math>\mathbf{a}_k = \ddot{\mathbf{r}}_k = \frac{d^2 \mathbf{r}_k}{dt^2} </math>

is the acceleration of the <math>
k
</math>-th particle, the second time derivative of its [[position vector]] <math>\mathbf{r}_k </math>. Each <math>\mathbf{r}_k </math> is expressed in terms of [[generalized coordinates]], and <math>\mathbf{a}_k </math> is expressed in terms of the generalized accelerations.

== Relations to other formulations of classical mechanics ==
Appell's formulation does not introduce any new physics to classical mechanics and as such is equivalent to other reformulations of classical mechanics, such as [[Lagrangian mechanics]], and [[Hamiltonian mechanics]]. All classical mechanics is contained within Newton's laws of motion. In some cases, Appell's equation of motion may be more convenient than the commonly used Lagrangian mechanics, particularly when [[Nonholonomic system|nonholonomic]] constraints are involved. In fact, Appell's equation leads directly to Lagrange's equations of motion.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Deslodge|first=Edward A.|date=1988|title=The Gibbs–Appell equations of motion|journal=American Journal of Physics|volume=56|issue=9|pages=841–46|doi=10.1119/1.15463|bibcode=1988AmJPh..56..841D |s2cid=123074999 |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01399766/file/EAD.pdf}}</ref> Moreover, it can be used to derive Kane's equations, which are particularly suited for describing the motion of complex spacecraft.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Deslodge|first=Edward A.|date=1987|title=Relationship between Kane's equations and the Gibbs-Appell equations|journal=Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics|publisher=American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics|volume=10|issue=1|pages=120–22|doi=10.2514/3.20192|bibcode=1987JGCD...10..120D }}</ref> Appell's formulation is an application of [[Gauss' principle of least constraint]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lewis|first=Andrew D.|date=August 1996|title=The geometry of the Gibbs-Appell equations and Gauss' principle of least constraint|journal=Reports on Mathematical Physics|volume=38|issue=1|pages=11–28|doi=10.1016/0034-4877(96)87675-0|bibcode=1996RpMP...38...11L |url=https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01401930/file/ADL.pdf}}</ref>

==Derivation==

The change in the particle positions '''r'''<sub>''k''</sub> for an infinitesimal change in the ''D'' generalized coordinates is

:<math>
d\mathbf{r}_{k} = \sum_{r=1}^{D} dq_{r} \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_{k}}{\partial q_{r}}
</math>

Taking two derivatives with respect to time yields an equivalent equation for the accelerations

:<math>
\frac{\partial \mathbf{a}_{k}}{\partial \alpha_{r}} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_{k}}{\partial q_{r}}
</math>

The work done by an infinitesimal change ''dq<sub>r</sub>'' in the generalized coordinates is

:<math>
dW = \sum_{r=1}^{D} Q_{r} dq_{r} = \sum_{k=1}^{N} \mathbf{F}_{k} \cdot d\mathbf{r}_{k} = \sum_{k=1}^{N} m_{k} \mathbf{a}_{k} \cdot d\mathbf{r}_{k}
</math>

where Newton's second law for the ''k''th particle

:<math>\mathbf{F}_k = m_k\mathbf{a}_k</math>

has been used. Substituting the formula for ''d'''''r'''<sub>''k''</sub> and swapping the order of the two summations yields the formulae

:<math>
dW = \sum_{r=1}^{D} Q_{r} dq_{r} = \sum_{k=1}^{N} m_{k} \mathbf{a}_{k} \cdot \sum_{r=1}^{D} dq_{r} \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_{k}}{\partial q_{r}} \right) = 
\sum_{r=1}^{D} dq_{r} \sum_{k=1}^{N} m_{k} \mathbf{a}_{k} \cdot \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_{k}}{\partial q_{r}} \right)

</math>

Therefore, the generalized forces are

:<math>
Q_{r} = 
\sum_{k=1}^{N} m_{k} \mathbf{a}_{k} \cdot \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_{k}}{\partial q_{r}} \right) =
\sum_{k=1}^{N} m_{k} \mathbf{a}_{k} \cdot \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{a}_{k}}{\partial \alpha_{r}} \right)
</math>

This equals the derivative of ''S'' with respect to the generalized accelerations

:<math>
\frac{\partial S}{\partial \alpha_{r}} = 
\frac{\partial}{\partial \alpha_{r}} \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{N}  m_{k} \left| \mathbf{a}_{k} \right|^{2} = 
\sum_{k=1}^{N} m_{k} \mathbf{a}_{k} \cdot \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{a}_{k}}{\partial \alpha_{r}} \right)
</math>

yielding Appell's equation of motion

:<math>
\frac{\partial S}{\partial \alpha_{r}} = Q_{r}.
</math>

==Examples==

===Euler's equations of rigid body dynamics===

[[Euler's equations (rigid body dynamics)|Euler's equations]] provide an excellent illustration of Appell's formulation.
 
Consider a rigid body of ''N'' particles joined by rigid rods.  The rotation of the body may be described by an [[angular velocity]] [[Vector (geometric)|vector]] <math>\boldsymbol\omega</math>, and the corresponding angular acceleration vector

:<math>
\boldsymbol\alpha = \frac{d\boldsymbol\omega}{dt}
</math>

The generalized force for a rotation is the torque <math>\textbf{N}</math>, since the work done for an infinitesimal rotation <math>\delta \boldsymbol\phi</math> is <math>dW = \mathbf{N} \cdot \delta \boldsymbol\phi</math>.  The velocity of the <math>k</math>-th particle is given by

:<math>
\mathbf{v}_{k} = \boldsymbol\omega \times \mathbf{r}_{k}
</math>

where <math>
\mathbf{r}_{k}
</math> is the particle's position in Cartesian coordinates; its corresponding acceleration is

:<math>
\mathbf{a}_{k} = \frac{d\mathbf{v}_{k}}{dt} = 
\boldsymbol\alpha \times \mathbf{r}_{k} + \boldsymbol\omega \times \mathbf{v}_{k}
</math>

Therefore, the function <math>
S
</math> may be written as

:<math>
S = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{N} m_{k} \left( \mathbf{a}_{k} \cdot \mathbf{a}_{k} \right)
= \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=1}^{N} m_{k} \left\{ \left(\boldsymbol\alpha \times \mathbf{r}_{k} \right)^{2} 
+ \left( \boldsymbol\omega \times \mathbf{v}_{k} \right)^{2} 
+ 2 \left( \boldsymbol\alpha \times \mathbf{r}_{k} \right) \cdot \left(\boldsymbol\omega \times \mathbf{v}_{k}\right) \right\}
</math>

Setting the derivative of ''S'' with respect to <math>\boldsymbol\alpha</math> equal to the torque yields Euler's equations

:<math>
I_{xx} \alpha_{x} - \left( I_{yy} - I_{zz} \right)\omega_{y} \omega_{z} = N_{x}
</math>

:<math>
I_{yy} \alpha_{y} - \left( I_{zz} - I_{xx} \right)\omega_{z} \omega_{x} = N_{y}
</math>

:<math>
I_{zz} \alpha_{z} - \left( I_{xx} - I_{yy} \right)\omega_{x} \omega_{y} = N_{z}
</math>
